The fight bled out of Phainon all at once. He sighed, stroking Snowy’s back with slow, tender motions.

Snowy leaned harder, stubborn in his smallness.

“…Okay, fine,” Phainon muttered, defeated. “One more hour. Just one more.”

The satisfaction radiating off Snowy was instant, though he buried it by tucking into Phainon’s neck like it wasn’t obvious.

Phainon narrowed his eyes at the halfhearted restraint. “You little cheat.” Fondness undercut every word. He wrapped both arms around Snowy, hauling him fully against his chest despite the squirm. “Might as well commit if you’re pulling this stunt.”

He buried his face into soft fur, petting with an almost aggressive fondness. “There. Now you’re stuck. Hope you’re happy, you cunning little fluffball.”

Snowy sighed, finally settling.

Phainon smiled into his fur, content against all reason.

It was finally the day.

Phainon had told himself it wasn’t a big deal—because it wasn’t. Mydei had gone on missions alone plenty of times before. This wasn’t new. He wasn’t going to make a fool of himself by waiting at the gates like some overeager puppy, glowing like he hadn’t had a minor panic spiral in front of a chimera. No. He had dignity. He could play it cool.

…Mostly.

He’d been pacing the Plaza for the better part of an hour, hands clasped behind his back, doing laps like a man training for some invisible marathon. Circle the fountain, glance at a stall, double back again. People had started giving him looks. He ignored them.

The one constant in his orbit was Snowy—shadowing him so close it was like he’d sprouted a second shadow. Every turn, every pause, there the chimera was, practically tripping his heels.

Phainon stopped mid-step, glanced down at him. “What, you nervous too? Or trying to herd me like a sheepdog?”

Snowy flicked his tongue.

Phainon raised a brow. “Don’t think I won’t get the staff involved. Impersonating livestock is a punishable offense.”

Snowy’s stare did not waver.

He sighed, a hint of laughter in it. “Fine. Come here, then.” With practiced ease, he scooped Snowy up, tucking him against his chest. “Let’s get some air. Maybe a better view will calm you down. Or me. Whichever.”

Snowy gave the smallest pout but didn’t resist when Phainon vaulted onto a nearby awning, then climbed to a higher ledge, until finally he perched on the broad rooftop overlooking Okhema. From here, the city stretched out in neat lines and bustle, the gates visible in the distance.

Phainon settled down cross-legged, setting Snowy on his lap. The chimera immediately claimed the spot, curling in like it had been reserved.

“See? Much better,” Phainon murmured, leaning back on his palms. “We wait here. Less humiliating than hovering at the entrance like some—” He cut himself off, mouth quirking. “Well. Like some lovesick fool.”

Snowy tilted his head up at him.

“What?” Phainon asked, straight-faced. “I’m perfectly composed. Dignified. Entirely calm.” A pause. “…You don’t believe me.”

Snowy’s soft chuff was answer enough.

“Mm. Treasonous little beast,” Phainon muttered, though his hand had already found Snowy’s fur, stroking idly down his back. “I feed you, I let you bully me into eating jerky for three days straight, and in return you question my honor? Scandalous.”

Snowy shifted, burrowing deeper into his lap.

Phainon exhaled a laugh, fingers brushing a tuft of fur smooth. “Thought so. Can’t stay mad at you, hm? You’re lucky I have a weakness for clingy, jealous little chimeras.” He said it lightly, almost distracted. “Otherwise I’d be very cross with you.”

The city clattered on below, carts rattling, vendors shouting. Up here, though, it was just the two of them—Snowy curled warm against him, and Phainon waiting, gaze fixed on the far gates with an expression he’d swear to anyone was casual.

The sound almost managed to lull him into something resembling calm.

Almost.

A prickle crept along the back of his neck, subtle but unmistakable.

Phainon kept his eyes trained on the horizon, posture as steady as if nothing at all had shifted. Only the faint exhale through his nose betrayed him, and with it came the quiet repositioning of his arm. Snowy was drawn closer, tucked firmly against him, the spread of his palm over the chimera’s side more protective than restraining.

“Easy,” he murmured. His thumb stroked through fur in a soothing line. “I’ve got you.”

Snowy moved—ears flicking, tail giving an irritated lash—but Phainon’s hand steadied him again before he could stir too much. Outwardly, his expression didn’t change. Yet the breath he drew in carried an edge that hadn’t been there before.

“Now…” His voice, when it came, was still calm, but sharpened just enough to cut. “Lady Cipher. As much as I understand your taste for this type of entertainment, I’d appreciate if you didn’t test them on me tonight. I’ve no patience for games.”

A pause stretched long enough to make the air feel heavier. Then, at his left, the rooftop shimmered—and laughter spilled out like someone slipping off a mask they hadn’t bothered to wear properly in the first place.

“‘Lady?’” Cipher echoed, suddenly perched against the edge of the roof as though she’d been lounging there all along. The grin she shot him was bright and shameless. “Please. You’re making me sound respectable. Loosen up, Deliverer—I was just saying hello to your little lap ornament.”

She wagged her fingers in Snowy’s direction. The chimera immediately let out a low growl from the safety of Phainon’s lap.

Cipher’s grin only widened. “Aw, see? He likes me.”

Phainon’s hand never faltered as it stroked Snowy’s fur once more. His reply was flat but not unkind. “Your definition of ‘like’ concerns me.”

She laughed at that, tilting her head, entirely unbothered by the rebuke. “Don’t be so stiff. If I wanted to snatch him, you wouldn’t even know I’d done it.”

At that, Phainon finally turned to look at her. Now usually he’d be nicer, but with Snowy involved? “And yet you announce it out loud.”

Cipher’s smile only grew, teeth flashing. “Well, what can I say? Where’s the fun if you don’t know?”

She stretched like a cat in a sunbeam, hands laced behind her head, and squinted at the drifting clouds.

“Really, Deliverer,” she drawled, tilting her head toward him without bothering to sit up. “You’re holding him like he’s porcelain. Are you sure that’s not your boyfriend in there?”

Phainon’s jaw tightened, but his expression stayed composed. “I don’t know what you mean,” he replied evenly. But his brows knit, just enough to betray the confusion he tried to suppress.

Snowy pressed closer into his lap, ears pinned flat, his golden eyes locked on Cipher. Phainon smoothed a hand over his head, murmuring with a dry edge, “See? He senses your mischief. Don’t encourage it.”

Cipher chuckled low in her throat and flicked a pebble from the rooftop, watching it arc lazily into the plaza below. She hummed a tune off-key, tapping her fingers on her knee, the very picture of idleness—except for the sly glint in her gaze when she slid her eyes back to them. “Scheming? Me?” she said innocently. “Perish the thought. I’m only here enjoying the view.”

“You’re circling him,” Phainon said humming. “Try not to act so much like a hawk over prey.”

That earned a sharp bark of laughter. She rolled onto her stomach, propping her chin on her fists as she leaned closer. “Oh? And what’s this little predator doing, then?” she teased, reaching out with mock affection. Snowy answered with a sudden snap of his teeth, the sound sharp in the air.

Cipher’s grin widened like a child who’d just been handed a new toy. “Feisty,” she purred. “I like him.”

Phainon sighed, rubbing behind Snowy’s ears to soothe him. “He’s better behaved than this usually,” he said, half exasperated, half amused—as though the irony weren’t lost on him that this was how Snowy chose to misbehave.

Cipher leaned back again, arms folded behind her head, all lazy composure. “He’s not misbehaving,” she said airily. “He’s hungry. That’s all.”

Phainon’s frown deepened. He glanced down at Snowy, who was still glaring with tense focus. “Hungry? Strange… I just fed him.”

With a theatrical flourish, Cipher produced something from thin air—or perhaps from a pocket no one had noticed. It gleamed strangely, metallic in the sun, too shiny to be normal food. She pinched it between her fingers, holding it out under Snowy’s nose with a wicked grin.

Phainon’s hand immediately swept in front of Snowy. “No. He doesn’t eat just anything. He’s picky enough with what I make as it is. And besides, I told you—he just ate.”

Snowy lunged suddenly, teeth grazing Phainon’s sleeve in his haste. Phainon jerked back, eyes flashing wide. “What—! Snowy, what has gotten into you?”

Cipher’s laughter rang out bright. “Oh, come now, Deliverer. Don’t look so scandalized. Even the pickiest eater has their weakness. Just let him have it.”

Her grin turned sharper as she waggled the treat again, waving it under Snowy’s nose like a dangling lure. “I promise—this one, he won’t refuse.”

“You can’t just feed strange things to someone else’s companion,” Phainon said firmly, leaning protectively over Snowy, his hand braced against the chimera’s chest.

“Relax.” Cipher shrugged, her voice sing-song but her eyes too sharp to match the carelessness. “It’s harmless. Just a snack. You really think I’d kill your precious pet?”

“No—” Phainon started.

Snowy snapped again, this time more desperate, more eager. And before Phainon could stop him, he snatched the morsel straight from Cipher’s fingers.

For a moment, silence. Then Phainon pressed his hand to his temple with a long sigh, defeated. “Very well. But if he gets sick, I’ll hold you personally responsible.”

Cipher only smirked, leaning back on her elbows. “I’ll take my chances. Enjoy him while you can, Deliverer.”

Phainon glanced down at Snowy, who chewed the gleaming treat with rapt delight, as though it were the best meal he’d ever had. “Impossible,” he muttered, though his hand still stroked the chimera’s fur with absent fondness.

To say Mydei made an appearance that afternoon would be a lie. Phainon stood under the sun until even the tile beneath his boots baked hot, the sky glaring down unrelenting. Hours passed. Nothing. No sign.

Snowy, curled in his arms, shifted restlessly, his body running hotter than it should. Phainon frowned, brushing damp hair from his temple as he adjusted his grip on the chimera. “Strange,” he muttered. “You’ve never minded the heat before.”

Snowy gave a faint growl, but it came out more like a weak whimper. He pressed closer, his body almost searing to the touch. Phainon adjusted him again, concern pricking sharper now.

(If only he knew—the little glimmer of Cipher’s handiwork had already begun to work its way through.)

By now, he should have gone to Aglaea. She always knew where to find Mydei, or at least had the right strings to tug. Truthfully, he was ready to set out himself, to comb the city stone by stone until he found the man. He had half a mind to do it—until his fingers brushed against his inner pocket.

There it was. A slip of parchment, folded twice over.

Patience, Deliverer. Your Prince Charming will be back in a few hours. You

might want somewhere private for the reunion—unless you prefer an

audience?

-Cipher

Phainon huffed. He couldn’t stay in his own quarters—he’d feel caged, pacing walls too narrow for the hours stretching ahead. And Snowy— burning as he was—needed more than stone and silence.

So he went to the one place that made sense.

Mydei’s residence.

How? He had a key. A key Mydei had pressed into his hand with a nod and a don’t lose it. Why Mydei had given it—Phainon had no idea. He’d never dared to ask.

Now, the door clicked open with a sound that felt far too intimate.

He should’ve sat. Instead, he paced, his boots moving grooves into the rug, his shoulders tense beneath his robes. Snowy, on the other hand, sprawled unceremoniously across the bed like he owned the place, the blankets bunching beneath his restless heat.

“You,” Phainon muttered, finally stopping long enough to lay the back of his hand against Snowy’s fur again, wincing at the warmth pulsing through. “You’re hotter than the sun itself.”

Snowy flicked an ear, the chimera equivalent of a stubborn glare, then huffed again, curling deeper into the pillows as if that solved everything.

Phainon sighed, stripping his outer layer of robes and fanning the air uselessly. “Of all times to burn like a forge,” he said, tone half-worried, half-exasperated. “You could’ve picked another season.”

Snowy answered with a glare.

Phainon dragged a hand down his face, then sat on the edge of the bed, restless knee bouncing. He leaned back, looking up at the ceiling with an exhale that refused to leave his chest. “If Cipher’s note was another trick…” he murmured, “then I swear—”

Snowy made a small sound, cutting him off—something oddly plaintive.

That alone silenced him.

He turned, softer this time, brushing Snowy’s fur with a gentler hand. “All right. Easy now. I’m here. Just… hold out a little longer, hm?”

Luckily, after barging into Mydei’s home and raiding every cupboard, Phainon found what he needed—a basin, a cloth, and water cold enough to sting his fingers. He wrung the towel out until it dripped, then laid it carefully across Snowy’s back.

The chimera twitched at first, tail flicking in protest, but gradually relaxed, the unnatural heat ebbing. Phainon didn’t dare look away, trading cloths as soon as they grew warm, hovering with the single-minded focus.

By the time an hour had passed, Snowy was finally cooling. His breaths evened out, no longer labored, his fur damp but less feverish to the touch.

“Thank the gods…” Phainon exhaled so hard his shoulders dropped. He slumped forward against the edge of the mattress, forehead resting there for a moment like all the tension was finally leaking out of him.

When he straightened again, brushing damp strands of hair from his face, his lips curved faintly upward. “…Well. Now that’s over with…”

Snowy cracked an eye open at him.

“Oh, don’t look at me like that,” Phainon muttered, then tapped his chin as if struck by a thought. “Actually, you know what? I’ve realized something.” His mouth quirked. “I’ve spent all this time with you, but I don’t know what you sound like when you’re not growling or hissing. At least meow once so I know what sound files I’m working with.”

Snowy’s ear twitched. That was it.

“…Not even a squeak? A chirp?” Phainon tried again, leaning closer. “A whistle? A honk?”

Nothing.

Snowy rolled his face away from him.

Phainon let out a long-suffering sigh and flopped forward in defeat. “You’re crueler than your master.”

Still, he couldn’t resist climbing onto the bed, sprawling beside Snowy until they were face to face. He braced his head against one palm, body angled toward him with a half-smile. “…Fine, whatever. I’ll stop bothering you.”

Snowy gave one smug look, the picture of victory.

For a few minutes, the quiet was companionable. But as the silence of Mydei’s empty home stretched on, the corners of Phainon’s good mood began to crumble. He sighed again—loudly, the tenth time today.

“…You mind if I overshare?” he asked the chimera softly.

Snowy made a weak, muffled grumble.

“I knew I could count on you,” Phainon said with a faint smile, then stared at the ceiling.

His voice started sharp, irritation dripping into every word: “Honestly, he should’ve been back hours ago. And when he finally does, I should give him an earful…” He tugged at his collar, scowling. “Though—gods. If he walked through that door right now, I’d probably let him do whatever he wants, as long as he’s safe.”

He didn’t even realize his words were softening until they already had.

“Stelle told me that meant I’d… what was it…” His brow furrowed as he muttered. “…‘Let him hit’—”

The sentence died halfway out of his mouth. His lips pressed together.

“…Never mind.”

Silence.

It took him two whole seconds to realize what he’d said. His head snapped toward Snowy. “…I didn’t mean it like that,” he blurted quickly.

Snowy didn’t dignify him with eye contact. The chimera simply angled his ears back, tail moving in a rhythm that screamed judgment.

Heat crawled up Phainon’s neck. “Oh, come on. Don’t give me that look. It’s not—” He coughed, rubbing awkwardly at the back of his neck. “… Anyway. Forget it. I didn’t—”

Snowy’s tail flicked harder.

Phainon groaned, throwing an arm over his face. “Great. Now even you think I’m pathetic.”

Snowy still wouldn’t look at him.

“Fine. Fine. I’m sorry, alright? I didn’t mean to—” His palm brushed Snowy’s fur again. He froze. “…Wait. Hold on—are you burning up again!?”

Snowy squirmed weakly, a soundless little noise leaving him. Phainon mistook it instantly for pain and gathered him up into his arms without hesitation. “Don’t fight me, I’ve got you,” he murmured, cradling the chimera. His brows furrowed tight with worry, his every muscle tense.

He sat there for a long stretch, fussing, pacing back and forth at the edge of the bed with Snowy in his arms, muttering half-coherent reassurances. Then, all at once, it dawned on him: Snowy’s heat wasn’t climbing anymore. In fact, he seemed steady. Relaxed.

Wait. Instead of a fever this time… was he just flustered?

Phainon froze, blinked twice—then laughed aloud, incredulous. “Hah! Sure, fine—laugh it up. I’m embarrassing, I know.” He sighed, letting his forehead tip forward until it brushed Snowy’s fur. “But as long as you’re alright, I don’t care.”

Snowy gave the faintest flick of his paw. Phainon took it as permission to keep holding him.

He adjusted his grip, scooping Snowy up like a spoiled housecat as he rose to his feet. With careful steps, he wandered toward the window, clutching him close. The world outside greeted him in bright colors—the sky clear, clouds lazily drifting, the courtyard below alive with the hum of a day untouched by his turmoil.

Phainon rested his chin against the crown of Snowy’s head, his voice low, almost wistful. “It’s a beautiful day, isn’t it?”

For a moment, there was peace. Warm sunlight across his shoulders. The quiet thrum of a heartbeat against his chest. The illusion of normalcy, the kind that made him forget anything had ever been strange.

Until Snowy stirred, writhing faintly. A pained noise left him, sharp enough to cut the calm. Phainon frowned immediately, pressing a soft kiss to the chimera’s cheek, half instinct, half distraction as he whispered, “What’s wrong now, hm? Talk to me—”

He didn’t get to finish.

The world buckled beneath him—not from a misstep, not from clumsiness, but from a sudden weight. Heavy, undeniable, crashing down from above. His knees buckled. Balance ripped away.

“—the hell!?”

They toppled. The air split with a thud and the crackle of displaced energy. Smoke erupted around them in a choking cloud, the acrid tang of something sweet curling in his throat. Phainon hit the floor flat on his back, the breath knocked out of him, his skull just shy of cracking against the boards.

Instinct took over. His arms locked tighter around where Snowy was, shielding him. Muscles coiled, ready to strike, to roll, to drive his elbow into the ribs of whatever had just ambushed them.

“Snow—!” His voice cracked with raw panic—

And then he saw.

Not an enemy. Not a beast.

A man.

Golden eyes burned above him, sharp as forged metal and startlingly close. A mane of beige hair framed his face, bleeding into crimson at the edges like wildfire taking hold. Tattoos traced crimson arcs over sun-dark skin, coiling down arms roped with strength. His lips—full, breath parted, trembling—moved as if to speak but stopped.

And his face—handsome enough to disarm armies—was flushed. Red-streaked, unsteady, embarrassed.

Phainon’s jaw unhinged. His mind went blank. His body forgot how to move. Why exactly? Because after a moment he realized, the fucking Crown Prince (King technically) of Castrum Kremnos—Mydeimos—was on top of him. Straddling him. Staring down at him with the rarest expression Phainon had ever seen: startled, cornered, human.

Time slowed. Smoke curled and dissolved. The silence pressed tighter and tighter, unbearably taut.

And then Mydei, resolute Mydei, fearless Mydei, opened his mouth.

“…Meow?”

Phainon’s brain had stalled out somewhere between golden eyes and uncharacteristically flushed. Everything past that was just static, static, static. He wasn’t mentally prepared to deal with this. Hell, he wasn’t even spiritually equipped to process this.

And of course, his traitor mind decided now—right now—was the perfect moment to serve him a memory from years ago, back when he’d been a wide-eyed, naive kid in Aedes Elysiae. Back when he thought being a hero was just… saving people and looking good while doing it.

Cyrene had been with him that day, perched cross-legged on a low stone wall with her book laid across her lap. She’d been “babysitting” him in her own words, but in reality she was mostly doodling crude little monsters into her book while he pestered her with hypotheticals.

Now that he thinks about it, she may have been high at the time.

“What if a basilisk looks me in the eye?” “Wear sunglasses.” “What if I’m outnumbered twenty to one?” ”Run faster than the slowest guy in your group.” “What if—” he’d paused, kicking a rock with all the solemnity of a child trying to understand mortality, “—what if I’m faced with something so strong I don’t even know what to do?”

Cyrene had beamed at him, eyes bright, tone the cheeriest it had ever been as she proclaimed the age-old wisdom passed down by absolutely no one but herself:

“Easy, Phainon. Knock yourself the fuck out.”

At the time, he’d laughed so hard he nearly fell over. No way in a thousand years would that ever be real advice. Who does that?

…Apparently him.

Because staring up now at Mydei—lips parted just slightly like the gods themselves had sculpted temptation—Phainon felt his entire nervous system revolt. His thoughts dissolved into white noise. His instincts shrieked at him to do something.

So he did the most natural thing in the world.

He lifted his head, smooth and graceful despite the chaos in his chest, and kept his golden eyes locked unblinking on Mydei’s. A dazed smile tugged at his lips, serene and unhinged all at once.

“Mydei, my guy,” he said faintly, voice thin with awe and delirium, “you’re just… too much.”

And then, without hesitation, he let his head fall back down. Violently.

The crack against the floor was sharp, echoing. A sting of pain bloomed, warm trickles of golden blood threading instantly through his hair.

Mydei’s face went from shocked to alarmed so fast it almost blurred.

Phainon, dimly aware that one knock probably wasn’t enough to do the job, twitched like he might go for round two. But before he could slam his skull again, strong hands caught his shoulders, holding him firmly in place.

“What are you—?!” Mydei’s voice cracked, horror plain as his eyes darted to the blood. “Deliv—stop!”

Phainon blinked up at him, half-lidded and dizzy, and thought with the kind of calm clarity only head trauma could grant: Nice. She was right.

Then the world went blissfully black.

The last thing he saw was Mydei’s mouth open mid-curse, panic etched across every line of his perfect face as he shouted his name:

“What the fuck, Phain—”

And then nothing.

The next time Phainon woke, the world didn’t so much return as drip back into him in reluctant droplets.

First came the smell. Acrid, sterile, and aggressively clean. Antiseptic. It crawled into his sinuses like an uninvited guest, stinging until he had no choice but to scrunch his nose. His throat cracked dry when he muttered, voice hoarse and gravelly:

“Gods above, who spilled an entire vat of bleach in here…?”

Second: the ceiling. He pried one eye open and immediately regretted it, but not before the image seared into his brain— endless white tiles, arranged in a grid of soul-crushing monotony. Each one freckled with pointless little dots, like some architect’s idea of whimsy was to make patients imagine seasoning their food.

“…Perfect,” he croaked.

Third: the blanket. He tried shifting his arms and discovered he could barely move. The sheets were tucked so tightly around him it felt like the mattress had swallowed him whole. He wiggled uselessly, shoulders straining, jaw clenched.

“Who—” he hissed, “—who tucked me in like a corpse? Was this necessary? What if I had to… defend myself? Or breathe? What if I wanted to itch my nose? Ever think about that?”

The sheets did not answer.

Grumbling, he decided to fight back in the only way he could think of: by sitting up. A bold move. A disastrous move.

The moment his head left the pillow, agony detonated across his skull. The pain was so sharp and sudden it felt like someone had shoved a war drum inside his brain and was beating it with iron hammers. His stomach lurched, the room tilted violently sideways, and he slammed back down onto the pillow with a groan that was equal parts curse and surrender. Both hands flew to his head like he could hold it together by force alone.

“Bad idea, bad idea, bad idea,” he gasped, squeezing his eyes shut until the brightness behind them dimmed to something survivable.

It took him a long moment to realize there was something tight around his skull. Bandages. Layers of them, snug, scratchy. His fingertips skimmed the rough edges automatically, feeling the ridges of wrappings that pressed against bruised skin. A patch on the left side was especially stiff, the fabric crusted with what was unmistakably dried blood.

“…Wonderful,” he muttered, tone flatter than parchment left in the sun.

His body felt heavy, as if they had to drag themselves uphill through syrup to reach him. Concussion fog, he realized dimly. He was concussed. That explained the pounding, the nausea creeping at the edges of his stomach, the weird way his vision refused to stay in one place for too long. He rubbed gingerly at his temple, like maybe pressing would unscramble the blurriness in his brain.

“Right,” he mumbled to himself, words tumbling out half-coherent, as though talking it through might anchor him. “I was at Mydei’s place. With Snowy. Window was nice. Day was nice. Snowy was… not nice. Then… weight. Smoke. Gold eyes. Red tattoos. And then—” he paused, lips pressing together, a faint grimace pulling at them. “Oh. Oh.”

If anyone else were here, they’d probably judge him for talking to himself.

But alas, there was no one.

He slumped back, dragging one palm over his face. “And then I decided to follow Cyrene’s age-old wisdom. ‘Knock yourself out,’ she says. Great advice. Brilliant. Inspired.”

A dry laugh escaped him, immediately cut short when it jostled the throbbing in his head. He groaned again and let his arm flop uselessly onto the stiff hospital sheets.

His vision swam if he blinked too fast. His ears rang faintly with every heartbeat. His stomach tilted like it couldn’t decide if it wanted to mutiny.

“…Yeah,” he whispered, drifting, “definitely concussed.”

Phainon should have gone back to sleep. That would’ve been the sensible thing. Close his eyes, let the throbbing lull him under again, and deal with everything later.

But of course, his brain—traitorous thing that it was—decided now was the perfect time to start thinking.

Too much time. Too many thoughts.

He exhaled slowly, staring at the pepper-speckled ceiling. What exactly did I see before I blacked out?

His hand slid up to press against the bandages as if squeezing them tighter might force out an answer.

“Okay,” he was starting to talk to himself, “let’s be rational about this. Step one. Was that real? Or a hallucination?”

A beat. His stomach flipped, not from nausea this time but from the memory.

“Oh no.” His voice cracked.

Because if it wasn’t a hallucination, then… then that meant…

“That means Snowy. Snowy. Turned into Mydei. And was straddling me.”

The words came out too loud in the quiet room. He immediately winced, as if the walls might judge him.

“Nope. Nope. Not thinking about that. Doesn’t matter. Not real. Totally hallucinated. Classic concussion symptom. Visual distortion. Common.” He nodded to himself a little too eagerly, then froze. But… but what if it was real?

The thought hit like a hammer to the chest.

Because if it was real, then how in all the gods’ names did Mydei turn into a chimera? And worse—worse—if Mydei was Snowy, then Phainon had very clearly and very dramatically declared his embarrassing, undying love for Mydei… directly to Mydei.

“Oh gods, oh gods, oh gods,” he groaned, dragging both hands down his face. The pain in his skull was nothing compared to the mortification creeping over every inch of him.

He kicked one leg under the too-tight sheets, wriggling like a trapped caterpillar, and finally gave in to the only defense mechanism left available.

Blanket. Over the head.

In one swift motion he yanked the stiff hospital sheet up to his chin, then over his nose, then all the way to his hairline until the world vanished into sterile-smelling darkness.

“Nope,” he mumbled into the fabric, voice muffled and pitiful. “Nope nope nope. Didn’t happen. Hallucination. Fever dream. Forget it. We’re forgetting it.”

He curled onto his side as best the wrappings and sheets would allow, burying his face deeper until his own breath warmed the cotton.

If anyone walked in right now, they’d find nothing but a lump in a hospital bed, hiding from reality itself.

Phainon intended to stay that way until the universe got bored and left him alone.

But alas, hiding under a blanket forever was impossible.

So Phainon got another idea.

A terrible idea.

“Right,” he muttered, peeling the blanket off his face with the sluggish dignity of someone crawling out of their own grave. “If I can’t un-think it… I’ll just… leave. Yes. Escape. Genius.”

Step one: standing.

He rolled his legs off the bed with all the grace of a sack of potatoes, braced both hands on the mattress, and shoved himself upright. His feet hit the floor, knees wobbled—and for a glorious two seconds, he thought hey, not so bad.

Then his legs reminded him they were currently made of warm custard.

He staggered three heroic, flailing steps forward before catching himself against the bedpost, forehead thunking against the wood. The room tilted sideways, then upside down. He squeezed his eyes shut until the nausea ebbed.

“…okay,” he wheezed, patting the bedpost. “Walking: not ideal.”

Step two: improvisation.

His gaze fell on the squat wooden chair beside the bed. A perfect walking stick. He grabbed it with both hands, wobbling in triumph—then froze mid-lift.

“No, no, bad idea. Chairs are for sitting. Chairs are for dignity.”

He shoved it back down.

Step three: nourishment.

The food tray on the bedside table glowed like a beacon of hope. He shuffled closer and found… beige porridge. A whole steaming bowl of the stuff.

He sniffed it cautiously. Bland. Lifeless. Utterly unremarkable.

Still, he poked at it with the spoon, lifted a bite, and shoved it into his mouth. A second later he gagged softly and pushed the tray away.

Step four: the door.

The brass handle gleamed at the far side of the room.

He inched toward it, one hand sliding along the wall for balance, until he reached the door. He wrapped trembling fingers around the handle and twisted gently.

Click.

Locked.

Phainon frowned, tried again. Jiggle. Jiggle. Nothing.

He pressed his ear to the wood, holding his breath.

Voices.

Muffled but clear enough—two of them, maybe healers, maybe guards.

“…took quite a blow to the head…”

“…concussion, but stable now…”

“…His Highness wouldn’t leave until we got the bleeding under control—”

Phainon jerked back from the door like it had sprouted teeth. His pulse spiked so hard it hurt.

His Highness.

Mydei.

Shit.

That meant Mydei had been here. Sitting at his bedside.

His stomach lurched. His bandaged head throbbed. His pride keeled over and died.

“That’s it,” Phainon hissed under his breath, clutching his skull. “Nope. Not facing him. Not happening. I’m getting out before he shows up and—gods forbid—talks to me.”

Step five: the only option left.

He turned his head toward the window.

The pale curtains fluttered faintly with the draft. Sunlight spilled across the sill. Beyond that: rooftops, sky, freedom.

It was the dumbest plan he’d ever had. Which, tragically, made it the most appealing.

He drew a shaky, dramatic breath.

“Screw it,” he muttered, steeling himself. “Window it is.”

And with that, Phainon began the slow, dizzy, utterly ridiculous trek toward freedom.

When he finally reached the sill, Phainon clung to the frame and pressed his forehead against the cool glass. The pane kissed back a faint chill, grounding him in a way that felt almost conspiratorial.

He curled his fingers under the latch. With a cautious tug, the window gave a complaining creak—then swung open without resistance.

Phainon blinked at it, then let out a soft laugh that immediately stung his ribs.

“…Huh. That was almost too easy.”

The curtains lifted in the draft, shifting around him in thin, whispering waves.

He leaned out far enough to look down—then outward.

Below, a respectable drop. Painful, sure, but survivable.

Across, another roof, close enough to leap if his legs weren’t trembling with fatigue.

Not the first time he’d made a questionable jump in worse conditions. He’d been drunker. Dizzy. Once with a head wound.

He’d be fine.

With a grunt, he hauled himself up onto the sill. His ribs protested; he ignored them, planting both palms firmly against the stone to catch his balance. The room behind him looked maddeningly cozy, like a trap disguised as comfort. The sky beyond stretched vast, endless, and more inviting than any bed.

He swung one leg over, settling his toes against the ledge, steadying himself with a shaky inhale.

Halfway there.

Another breath. He could do this.

“See? Easy,” he murmured to no one but himself. “Just a little jump. Land, run, never see—”

Then the door creaked.

Soft. Careful.

The sound of a hand on the latch, turning slow, easing it open as if not to wake a sleeping body.

Phainon froze, one leg dangling into the open air, his head snapping toward the noise.

The door inched wider. A shadow eased into the room, stretching long across the floorboards.

“…Are you awake, Deliver—?”

The voice was quiet, cautious, every syllable laid down with the tenderness of someone afraid to intrude.

Phainon’s heart dropped hard into his stomach.

He hadn’t turned yet. He didn’t need to. The warmth in that tone was unmistakable.

For one suspended second, the room was held in softness—the prince lingering in the doorway, shoulders curved slightly as though he’d meant only to peek in, to check if Phainon was comfortable, if he needed anything. His presence filled the chamber without crowding it, the gentleness in his expression so at odds with everything Phainon had been preparing for.

Phainon almost convinced himself he could brazen it out. Pretend. Joke. Maybe Mydei would back out the way he came if he thought Phainon was asleep.

But then—

A rush of air.

The curtains snapped wild against the frame, the open window suddenly swallowed by something faster.

Hands seized his waist.

The strength behind them was terrifying in its ease. Phainon was plucked clean off the sill and hauled backward in a single, fluid motion, like he weighed no more than a cloak being gathered from a hook. His body collided against the heat of a chest he knew instantly, the solid wall of muscle and steadiness anchoring him whether he wanted it or not.

His breath caught in a startled choke. “What—?”

The grip didn’t loosen.

Twisting slightly, he craned his neck back—and found himself staring up at exactly who he’d hoped not to see.

Mydei.

He didn’t want to look at him. Didn’t want to see what expression waited there.

But he did.

And in that instant, the prince’s gentleness—so clear just moments ago in the doorway—was gone.

What replaced it was restraint wound razor-tight, anger pulled taut across every line of his face. His jaw set hard. His eyes, usually so steady, blazed with a furious clarity. Every inch of him radiated not irritation for its own sake, but frustration sharpened by concern: for Phainon specifically.

The difference was startling. Almost unbearable to look at.

“What is wrong with you.”

It wasn’t loud. It didn’t need to be.

The measured tone struck hotter than fire, the syllables curling through Phainon’s chest and leaving no room to laugh it off.

His throat bobbed. His pulse thundered. He couldn’t—wouldn’t—do this right now.

So, like any rational man staring down death in the shape of a furious Mydeimos, he tried the smallest, dumbest thing possible: easing sideways, wriggling with mock-nonchalance, as though he might simply slip free if he played casual enough.

Mydei’s hold answered before words did.

It tightened.

Not enough to cause pain—just firmly, irrevocably, enough to crush the very thought of escape in its cradle.

Slowly, Mydei guided Phainon away from the window. Phainon shuffled along, legs heavy and unreliable, the dizziness clinging to him stubborn as smoke.

“You make a terrible jailer,” he muttered, aiming for levity though his voice sounded thinner than he wanted. He craned his neck just enough to try to catch Mydei’s face. “Could’ve just asked nicely, you know. Something polite. ‘Dearest Deliver, would you mind not throwing yourself out a window today?’”

Mydei didn’t dignify that with an answer. Just that look—absolutely unimpressed, a quiet dismissal of his jokes.

Phainon winced.

Finally, Mydei exhaled through his nose, sighing. “Would you have listened?”

For a moment, Phainon almost laughed. The corner of his mouth quirked instead. “I’d like to think so. I’m very reasonable you know.”

When they reached the bed , Mydei pressed him down—not violent, but firm enough that Phainon’s knees gave in with a grunt. He fell back onto the mattress, letting out a half-muffled laugh at the indignity of being manhandled like a stubborn child.

He wriggled to get comfortable, tugged at the blanket, then started tapping his fingers restlessly against his thighs. Anything to keep his eyes busy. Anything to avoid the steady weight of Mydei’s gaze.

The silence stretched.

“Why did you think escaping like that was a good idea?” Mydei asked at last, his voice edged with sternness. “And the head thing—were you honestly trying to knock yourself out or was there something else? Tell me, Deliverer. Are you actually that stupid?”

Phainon chuckled weakly. “Not stupid,” he said, though his voice faltered like it couldn’t quite commit. He shifted, tugging the blanket higher, curling into the weight of the bed. His laugh caught in his throat. “Just… inventive.”

Mydei didn’t look convinced. He leaned slightly forward, obviously about to get to the point.

“…Don’t. Please,” Phainon whispered, the levity slipping at last. He stared at the folds of the blanket, his voice catching.

Mydei tilted his head. “Don’t what?”

Phainon exhaled shakily, then glanced away. “Don’t press me about what I said earlier. Not right now.” The words spilled out faster than he meant them to, and he rushed to tack on before Mydei misunderstood, “I’m not dodging it! I promise. We’ll talk about it—really talk about it. Just…” His fingers tapped faster on his thigh. “Not now. My head’s still foggy. And you —” he swallowed, forcing himself to look briefly at Mydei before glancing away again “—you deserve an actual conversation. Not whatever garbled nonsense I’d spit out like this.”

The embarrassment in his voice gave it a rough edge, but the sincerity beneath it was impossible to miss.

He tugged the blanket again, then softened, speaking quieter. “Please? Let me… let me give you the kind of answer you deserve. Not the half-mangled one I’d give while my brain’s trying to leak out my ears.”

The silence returned, but it didn’t feel empty. Mydei studied him for a moment. Phainon’s fingers drummed against his thighs like a heartbeat, waiting.

Finally, Mydei’s hand came to rest against his shoulder. Not holding, just a touch that grounded. His expression softened, and after a pause, he nodded once.

“Alright. I’ll wait.”

No pressure or conditions added on. Just patience.

Phainon felt something unclench in his chest, a weight he hadn’t realized he’d been dragging. Mydei’s voice always carried a sort of calmness. Somehow, it always managed to soothe Phainon.

Exhaustion crept back in, dragging heavy at Phainon’s limbs. He fought it stubbornly, smirking faintly as his head lolled against the pillow.

Mydei, of course, noticed. “Lay down properly, HKS,” he murmured, eye twitching. “You’re making a mess of it.”

Phainon closed one eye lazily. “Bossy,” he muttered, but the smirk stayed.

A moment of quiet passed, soft enough that Phainon thought maybe Mydei would leave it there. But then his voice came again, deceptively casual:

“…Unless you’d like to explain who exactly this ‘Alexander’ is?”

Phainon groaned aloud this time and promptly shut his eyes as tight as possible, feigning sleep with all the dignity of a child pretending they couldn’t hear their name being called.

The silence that followed cracked only with the softest sound: a quiet snort of laughter. Mydei shifted closer, and a moment later Phainon felt the brush of fingers against his hair, sweeping it gently off his forehead.

“Go to sleep, HKS,” Mydei whispered, softer than the air between them. “I’ll see you tomorrow.”

The warmth of the words sank into him, and this time Phainon didn’t resist. Sleep pulled him down fully, the quiet wrapping around him like a promise.

With any luck, he’d survive facing Mydei when he woke.

Tomorrow would come soon enough.
